1.pericope_label: The appointed feasts and the sabbath at their head

schools.summary: Gill places the chapter after the laws of holiness for people, priests and sacrifices, and reads the six days as days on which lawful work may be done.

Henry argues that only divine appointment can make time holy, prefers the rendering "solemnities" because the day of atonement was a fast, and reads the public convocation as serving both the honour of God and the edification of the people.

Clarke explains the word for feast as any solemn anniversary and makes the sabbath the threshold of all religion; Wesley independently presses the same distinction between all work and servile work, and notes that the sabbath alone was kept in every dwelling rather than at Jerusalem.

Ellicott gives a closer rendering of the opening formula, calls the sabbath the oldest festival, cites a rabbinic saying that it equals the whole law, and distinguishes the total prohibition of work on it from the ban on servile work at the other feasts, tracing the later rules and their relaxation for sickness; Keil and Delitzsch set the sabbath at the head of the seasons because God sanctified it at creation, which marks it off from feasts commemorating Israel’s history.

debates: Whether "these are my feasts" should be rendered feasts, assemblies or solemnities, Henry preferring the last because one of them is a fast.
outliers: Ellicott and Wesley arrive independently at the same argument from the difference between "no work" and "no servile work".
Ellicott records the second-Temple ruling that danger to life suspends the sabbath prohibition, and compares it with Christ’s saying.

4.pericope_label: The passover and the seven days of unleavened bread

schools.summary: Gill dates the passover by the month of the exodus and explains the unleavened bread from the haste of the departure; Calvin assigns the institution of the passover to the first commandment and its annual recurrence to the fourth.

Henry traces the feasts to divine appointment against Jeroboam’s invention, explains the choice of months by the convenience of travel and harvest, and counts six days of holy joy against one of mourning.

Ellicott repeats the heading as marking off the festivals proper from the sabbath and supplies the later practice in detail — the hours of stopping work, the signal for burning leaven, the pilgrimage obligation and its radius, the scale of the crowds, the private offerings and the permitted work of the intervening days; Keil and Delitzsch ground the distinction between total and servile prohibition in two different Hebrew expressions.
Wesley again prefers "solemnities" to "feasts" because one of them is a fast.

debates: Under which commandment the passover belongs, Calvin distinguishing the rite, which he treats under the first, from the yearly festival, which he places under the fourth.
outliers: Ellicott reports an eye-witness estimate of some two and a half million at a single passover, and compares the encampment outside the walls with the modern pilgrimage to Mecca.
Ellicott notes that breaking the festival rest was punished with stripes rather than with the stoning prescribed for sabbath-breaking.

9.pericope_label: The sheaf of firstfruits waved before the Lord

schools.summary: Calvin argues that a handful rather than a measure is meant, distinguishes the waving from the heave motion, and makes the rite a guard against the heathen deification of the earth, since the whole harvest was consecrated in one handful without any of the people’s food being diminished; Gill describes the motion of the waving and rejects the Jewish account of the doubled meat offering in favour of thankfulness proportioned to mercies.

Wesley denies that the offering was made in the ear or by handful at all, has the priest wave it in the name of the whole congregation, and adopts the twofold explanation of the doubled measure that Gill rejects; Clarke has the sheaf waved before the people to stir their gratitude, and notes that parched and green ears are still eaten in the country.

Ellicott treats the omer ritual as a prospective law added to the passover, describes how the corn was selected and tied the day before, details the priest’s handling of it, and reports the second-Temple extension of the prohibition to five kinds of new grain and its parallels among other nations.

debates: What was actually brought and offered: a handful (Calvin), a measured omer of meal (Ellicott, Gill), or grain cleaned of chaff, dried and beaten out (Wesley).
Before whom the sheaf was waved, Gill and Wesley saying before the Lord and for the congregation, Clarke saying before the people to call their attention to providence.

Why the meat offering was of double the usual measure: because the harvest was plentiful (Gill, Ellicott) or because one part belonged to the lamb and one to the corn (Wesley, and the Jewish authorities Gill cites).
outliers: Calvin treats the rite as a deliberate barrier against making the earth herself the mother of gods and men.

15.pericope_label: Pentecost, the two wave loaves, and the gleanings for the poor

schools.summary: Gill defends the sixteenth of Nisan as the starting point, reports the rabbinic dispute over the manner of waving, and prefers charity to the poor over the rabbinic praise of gleaning as equivalent to building the sanctuary.

Henry contrasts this feast with the firstfruits at every point — a handful against two loaves, unleavened against leavened, one lamb against many — and reads the sin offering as a confession of unworthiness.

Clarke gives the reckoning in dates from the sixteenth of the first month; Wesley resolves the discrepancy with Numbers by liberty of choice or a division of function, presses the singular in the gleaning law on every individual, and makes the outpouring of the Spirit the perfection of the feast.

Ellicott renders the interval as seven weeks and supports it from Hebrew and Greek usage, records the modern counting of the omer, describes the baking and waving of the two loaves in detail, harmonises this list of victims with the one in Numbers by referring them to the wilderness and the land respectively, and traces the feast’s later transformation into the commemoration of the giving of the Law; Keil and Delitzsch explain the larger offerings from the character of the feast as a thanksgiving for the whole harvest and read the gleaning law as placed here on purpose.

debates: How the victims listed here are to be reconciled with the different list in Numbers: two distinct sets of sacrifices for wilderness and land (Ellicott), or a liberty of choice, or a division between the feast day and the loaves (Wesley).
Whether the sabbath from which the fifty days are counted is the weekly one or the opening day of the feast, which Gill argues for expressly.
outliers: Wesley and Ellicott independently connect the feast with the giving of the Law, Wesley adding Pentecost in Acts as its perfection.
Keil and Delitzsch read the law of the corners and gleanings as deliberately placed inside the harvest feast.

23.pericope_label: The feast of trumpets on the first of the seventh month

schools.summary: Gill details who was bound to hear the trumpets and how many soundings were required; Calvin denounces the Jewish account that the day commemorates the deliverance of Isaac, allows that others rightly make it a preparation for the atonement, and prefers to see in it a yearly reminder that all sacred assemblies are called by the voice of God.

Henry treats the day as the old new year, describes the sounding from sunrise to sunset, and canvasses the trumpet at Sinai and the creation of the world as what is remembered, noting the Aramaic rendering "a memorial of shouting".

Clarke takes the feast simply as the opening of the civil year and passes on the suggestion about creation; Wesley makes the seventh month a sabbatical month whose opening trumpets prepare the people for the fast and the feasts within it.

Ellicott renders the phrase "remembrance blowing", takes it of Israel being remembered before God, reports the synagogue’s contrary sense of reminding God of the patriarchs and the lessons appointed accordingly, and describes the threefold sacrifice and the order of the day’s service.

debates: What the trumpets commemorate: Sinai or the creation (Henry, Clarke), Israel’s remembrance before God (Ellicott), the deliverance of Isaac (the synagogue tradition Ellicott reports and Calvin denounces as baseless), or nothing beyond the summons of God’s own voice (Calvin).
Whether the day has an independent character or exists as a preparation for the day of atonement, which Calvin allows and Ellicott assumes.
outliers: Calvin rejects the Isaac tradition in unusually sharp terms, while Ellicott records without comment that the lessons for the day are the birth and binding of Isaac.
Wesley makes the seventh month a sabbatical month on the analogy of the seventh day and the seventh year.

26.pericope_label: The day of atonement: affliction of soul and total rest

schools.summary: Gill explains the introductory formula and its omission before pentecost, records the exemption of the sick and the young from the fast, and reads the repeated prohibition as a measure of God’s strictness; Calvin derives the plural "atonements" from the manifold guilt requiring reconciliation, describes the day as a citation before God’s tribunal, and argues from the severity of the penalty that a humbled heart is what pleases God, with the man who has shaken off fear and shame beyond hope.

Ellicott marks this as the only day besides the sabbath forbidding all work, notes that the threat uses "destroy" rather than "cut off" while carrying a lighter penalty than sabbath-breaking, explains the repetitions as emphasis, and faults the translators for varying a formula the Hebrew keeps constant; Keil and Delitzsch set out the fast from evening to evening and the rest on pain of death.

Wesley adds repentance for national sins and particularly the golden calf, reads the threat as showing every man’s need of forgiveness, and contrasts the Jewish reckoning of the day from evening in memory of creation with the Christian reckoning from morning in memory of the resurrection.

debates: Whether the stronger word "destroy" implies a heavier penalty, Ellicott noting that sabbath-breaking was punished by stoning while this offence was punished only by excision.
outliers: Calvin makes the fast a formal appearance before God’s tribunal in which the worshipper concedes the sentence and pleads against its execution.
Wesley suggests the golden calf as the national sin chiefly to be remembered on the day.

33.pericope_label: The feast of tabernacles and its eighth day

schools.summary: Calvin contrasts the passover’s memory of a single rescue with this feast’s memory of forty years of continuing grace, explains why Zechariah requires the nations to keep this feast in particular, leaves the etymology of the closing day open, and reads the caution about the ordinary sacrifices as a guard against transferring what was already owed; Gill describes the present-day observance with the palm bundle and citron.
Henry makes the fast a preparation for the joy of this feast and the feast a recompense for the fast.

Clarke collects pagan festivals of tents, including a writer who inferred from this feast that the Jews worshipped Bacchus; Wesley makes the eighth day the great day of the feast and reads the move from booths into houses as figuring the settlement in Canaan.

Ellicott notes that the law leaves the construction of the booths undefined and supplies the later rules, and alone records the drawing of water at Siloam, the willow canopy and the nightly illumination, supposing Christ spoke of himself when it was about to be extinguished; Keil and Delitzsch derive the name of the closing day from shutting in and reject the two alternative derivations; Ellicott explains "sabbaths" as standing by metonymy for the sabbath sacrifices.

debates: What the name of the closing day means, where Calvin allows both "restraint" and "solemn assembly" and leaves the choice to the reader, while Keil and Delitzsch rule out both in favour of the sense of closing a festival.
outliers: Clarke reports an ancient inference that the Jews worshipped Bacchus because his vintage festival was also called the feast of tabernacles.
Wesley and Ellicott both connect the eighth day with the Gospel scene at the feast, Wesley through the invitation to the thirsty and Ellicott through the extinguishing of the great illumination.

39.pericope_label: Booths, branches, and the reason for the feast

schools.summary: Gill reports the citron identification and the rules about ownership, and records the parting prayer to dwell next year in the booth of Leviathan; Calvin refuses to take the word for a proper name and keeps its ordinary sense of comeliness, and makes the branches a signal of gladness and a foretaste of heaven for men still sojourning.

Clarke accepts the citron and myrtle and finds in the feast a double object of memory and gratitude, calling an ungrateful heart unfeeling and disobedient; Wesley denies that this is a new law, defines the ingathering as the fruit of the trees rather than the corn, identifies the trees from the account of the post-exilic celebration, and ends by contrasting the burden of these feasts with the lighter Christian ones.

Ellicott treats these verses as a supplementary enactment, explains how the second-Temple authorities identified the goodly fruit as the citron and defined the palm shoot, and reads the yearly week under branches as a reminder to a settled people of how their fathers were sheltered.

debates: What the "boughs of goodly trees" are: the citron, on the second-Temple definition (Gill, Clarke, Ellicott); any attractive and comely tree, the word being no proper name (Calvin); or the olive, myrtle and pine named at the post-exilic celebration (Wesley).
outliers: Gill records that those leaving the booths prayed to be found worthy next year of the booth of Leviathan, meaning the messianic feast, and that a ninth day was later added for the completion of the reading of the law.
Calvin makes the booths a foretaste of the life of heaven on the ground that those who kept the feast were themselves only sojourners on earth.
